queries.query: We just acquired a startup and inherited their frontend codebase at `https://github.com/acme-corp/customer-portal`. Before we start integrating it into our main platform, I need you to do a deep dive on the repo and give me a full architectural breakdown — what framework and version they're using, their state management approach, routing strategy, component organization patterns (atomic design, feature-based, etc.), build toolchain (bundler, transpiler, dev server), package manager and lockfile format, whether they're using TypeScript and how strictly, CSS strategy (modules, styled-components, Tailwind, etc.), testing frameworks, linting/formatting setup, and any monorepo tooling. Also flag any outdated or deprecated dependencies that could be a migration risk. I'd like the output in three formats: (1) an executive summary I can forward to our VP of Engineering, (2) a detailed technical breakdown with dependency tree highlights, and (3) a visual diagram showing the architecture layers and how data flows through the app. If you spot any anti-patterns or architectural debt, call those out explicitly with severity ratings.

Help me plan and spec out a new feature for our Vue 3 + TypeScript app at `~/repos/fleet-dashboard` — we need a real-time vehicle tracking map view with Pinia stores for vehicle state, composable hooks for WebSocket connections, and Vue Router nested routes for drill-down panels. Before writing any code, I'd like to create a proper specification, break it into atomic testable tasks, and define an implementation plan. The app uses Vite, `<script setup>`, and we want to make sure everything follows modern Vue conventions. Can you walk me through the full structured engineering process — intent, context, spec, plan, and tasks — and then show me how the key `.vue` components and stores should be structured?

We have a Go microservice at `~/repos/api-gateway/` that proxies requests to about a dozen downstream services. Right now every upstream client can hammer any endpoint without limits and we've already had two outages from a single misbehaving partner flooding our `/transactions/bulk` endpoint. I need you to design and implement a robust rate limiting layer as middleware. Requirements: per-API-key limits with different tiers (free: 100 req/min, pro: 1000 req/min, enterprise: 10k req/min), a sliding window log algorithm for accuracy, a token bucket fallback for burst tolerance on the enterprise tier, and since we run 8 replicas behind an ALB, the counters need to be shared via our existing Redis Cluster (already configured in `config/redis.go`). Also, the rate limit headers (`X-RateLimit-Remaining`, `X-RateLimit-Reset`, `Retry-After`) need to be set on every response. When a client is throttled, return a `429` with a JSON body that includes how many seconds until their window resets. Finally, add a `/internal/rate-limits` admin endpoint that shows current consumption for all active API keys so our ops team can monitor abuse in real time. Can you scaffold this out with tests that simulate concurrent requests from multiple keys hitting the limits?

We're scaling our outbound sales motion and I want to build a systematic cold email testing framework in Python at `~/repos/outreach-engine/`. Here's what I need: create a module that manages multi-variant cold email campaigns where we can define subject lines, opening hooks, CTAs, and email body templates as independent variables, then assign prospects to test cells using proper randomization with configurable traffic splits (e.g., 80/20 holdout or even splits across variants). It should track opens, replies, and positive replies per variant, calculate statistical significance using a two-proportion z-test so we know when we have a real winner vs. noise, and flag when we've hit minimum sample sizes for each cell. I also want a `results_dashboard.py` script that outputs a summary table showing each variant's conversion rate, confidence intervals, lift over control, and p-values — plus recommendations on whether to keep testing or declare a winner and roll out. Make sure the system supports sequential testing so we're not just peeking at results and fooling ourselves with false positives. We've been burned before by calling winners too early on 50-email samples and then seeing performance revert.

We're running a data analytics platform on AWS and our monthly bill has ballooned from ~$14K to $47K over the past six months without a proportional increase in traffic or customers. Here's what we're running: 3 x r6i.4xlarge RDS instances (Multi-AZ) for what I think are mostly read-heavy workloads, about 40 ECS Fargate tasks across staging and production (some of which I suspect are orphaned from old feature branches), a NAT Gateway that's showing 8TB/month of data processing charges, a fleet of m5.2xlarge EC2 instances in an ASG that scales between 6-20 but CloudWatch shows they rarely go above 35% CPU utilization even during peak, about 15TB in EBS gp2 volumes (some possibly unattached), and we're paying on-demand for everything — no RIs, no Savings Plans, no spot usage whatsoever. We also have three ElastiCache r6g.xlarge nodes and an OpenSearch domain with 3 master + 6 data nodes that was set up for a logging pipeline we partially migrated to Datadog six months ago. Can you help me put together a comprehensive cost optimization plan with specific recommendations, estimated savings percentages for each area, and a prioritized implementation roadmap? I'd like concrete instance type suggestions, a strategy for which workloads should go on Savings Plans vs. spot, and guidance on identifying and eliminating the waste.

Our team maintains `mobile-checkout-sdk` on GitHub and we've accumulated about 150 PR review comments over the past week across 23 merged pull requests. Can you pull all the review comments from the last 7 days, analyze them, and produce a structured weekly code-review digest document? I'd like it to surface recurring themes (e.g., are reviewers constantly flagging the same null-safety issues or naming convention violations?), group repeated issues by category with frequency counts, highlight any architectural concerns that came up in multiple PRs, and end with a concrete "Top 5 Takeaways" section the team can reference in our Monday standup. Format it as a Markdown doc we can drop into our `docs/review-digests/` folder with the date in the filename.

We have a phased implementation plan (attached as `plan.md`) for "AetherVault," a decentralized file storage startup's new marketing site built with Next.js 14, React Three Fiber, and Framer Motion. The plan has 5 phases: (1) project scaffolding & design tokens, (2) hero section with an interactive 3D crystalline vault animation that responds to scroll, (3) feature comparison grid with bold split-screen layouts and kinetic typography, (4) pricing page with fluid morphing card transitions, and (5) testimonials carousel with parallax depth effects. I need you to execute all 5 phases from the plan, figuring out which phases can run in parallel vs. which have hard dependencies. But here's the critical part — before committing to any design direction for each phase, I want you to run an internal debate between at least three opposing viewpoints: a brutalist minimalist who thinks most animation is gratuitous noise, a maximalist creative director who wants every pixel to feel alive, and a UX accessibility advocate who'll push back on anything that sacrifices usability for flash. Let them genuinely argue it out for each phase's key design decisions (color palette, animation intensity, spatial layout, typography scale) and document the consensus or winning argument before you write the code. The final output for each phase should be production-ready components — no placeholder boxes, no generic gradients, no safe corporate blue. I want the kind of landing page that makes other founders screenshot it in Slack. Use unexpected color pairings, oversized type, and spatial compositions that feel architectural rather than templated.

We're about to ship a set of custom Webflow Code Components (a React-based card carousel and an interactive pricing calculator) via `webflow library share`, but before we do, I need two things handled in one pass. First, run a full pre-deployment validation on both components — check the bundle sizes are under Webflow's limits, verify all prop configurations and slot definitions are correct, confirm there are no SSR-incompatible hooks or browser-only APIs in the initial render path, make sure our Tailwind styles aren't leaking globally, and flag any dependency issues (we're importing `framer-motion` and `recharts` so I want to know if those bloat the bundle or break in Webflow's runtime). Second, we deploy these components through an Ansible playbook that provisions a staging Webflow workspace and pushes environment-specific API keys (Stripe publishable keys, analytics IDs, and a CMS read token) into the component config. Right now the keys are hardcoded in `group_vars/all.yml` as plain text, which is terrible. I need you to refactor the playbook to pull all secrets from our Infisical vault using a reusable lookup task pattern, add `no_log: true` on every task that handles credentials, and set up a fallback chain so if Infisical is unreachable it tries the local encrypted vault file before failing. Show me the complete validated component checklist plus the refactored playbook with the secrets integration.

hypothesis: Unconditional fixed equal-weight RRF60 of cached SkillRet and Jev Score ranks improves NDCG@10; ties preserve dense order.
question_type: Score only,20 fixed header-only questions per query
selection: First8 salted SHA256 query IDs with salt mia5150-fixed-rrf-confirmation-v1:, exclude all128 prior scorer IDs and the eight selective-panel IDs; no qrels inspection.
parameters: One hypothesis, RRF60 equal weight; no sweep, no rerun, no reordering candidates from labels.
failure_policy: Stop at first uncertain failure; failed/unattempted predictions empty, all8 retained; no provider fallback or retries.
exposure: New to this round and excluded previous rerank cohorts, but historically exposed public benchmark, including full4392 dense evaluation. Not a genuine blind final test.
